blocks.x: If you're ready, we can start off. We'll start off until the date. This is March 1st, 1961. What is the address here?
2401 Orleans Street.
Yes, and this is Mr. Thompson's home, and Harold Dajon and Ralph Collins and Bill Russell are here interviewing Mr. Thompson. Can you give your full name?
William Thompson.
Can you tell us just when you were born and where it was?
I was born 1895, 28th of June. Right here in New Orleans.
Right here. Is it in this neighborhood or around?
No, on Claybone Street.
On Claybone.
Claybone to the Abbeville and Vemma.
Not far from here, right? No. Can you tell us a little bit about your folks, if anybody in the family played any music, your father or mother, anybody playing?
My father used to be a banjo player.
Oh, banjo.

Yeah, he used to be playing music on a camellia. Oh, on the boat? At the West End, yeah. On the scene, but, uh... Was that the band? At the West End, yeah, he had a band. He used to play out there, play banjo.
Do you remember whose band it was or who else he played with?
Oh, Joe Murphy's one band, I don't remember. In the band? The other one, I don't know who was. The other one was there.
What did he play at, Joe Murphy?

Joe Murphy was, uh, playing, uh, Conant. He used to play conant. He'd be, uh, bandjoe sometime himself. And, uh... Later on, when they left from the West End, they went to Millen Boy. Oh, yeah. I drove to Millen Boy, you know. And play on the boat from there. Uh-huh. Uh-huh. Go out to the lake, you know. Yeah. Run all around the lake.
Did he go across?
A few hours. Sometimes go across the lake and back. Uh-huh. On the pleasure boats.
Yeah.
And play.
Did he have any piano in the house? Uh, how did you get started on piano?
Well, I got started on piano through my brother. I had a brother called Joby.
Was he older?
Yeah, he was older than me. He used to play piano.
Oh.
All around. And I picked it up from him. I was about... Oh, about ten years old when I started playing piano.
Uh, is he still living, or...?
No, my brother died. About four or five years ago.
What, what?
Uh, to go around town and playing all around, different places.
Did he play mostly by himself, or in any band? Do you remember?
No, he played mostly by himself, just going from place to place like that, playing. And I picked it up a while, and I started playing around the house, boys.
Where did you find the piano to practice on or learn? Where did you...
Well, at the house. I had one there. My brother had one. Oh, your brother had one. Yeah. I started playing there. Pick it up.
Did you have any lessons, or anybody help you besides your brother?
No. Never took no lessons. Just went on and played.
Did he help you any, or just you watched him?

And then, now that he'd be sitting down, I'd be looking at him, he'd tell me, boy, there ain't a way to play that. He'd say, you play this a way. Yeah. Yeah. I'd go out and play it the way he played, and then I'd take and make it my way. I'd go and play it my way.
Do you remember what kind of pieces you played when you started out?
Oh, I played most ragtime, blues. It was the most other thing that I could whistle. I'd play anything.
What was the first time that you ever played for anybody else, any kind of a job or party or anything? Do you remember what it was?

Oh, I played in house parties around. I played at a place called Old Mill Street. It was on Cronlite Walk between Broad and White. I played there. I remember that being about one of the first jobs I was playing piano back there.
Cronlite Walk, that's Lafitte Street now. Yeah, that's Lafitte Street. I see where no bass in was there. It was Cronlite Walk.
I played along there. And from that, I just went on from house to house. I played at Melon Boy. At Lucian's Pavilion out there.
Somebody else said that Lucian's Pavilion was next to Boundary.
At the lake.
Bruce had said the other day that he played out of Lucian's too, I believe. Yeah, Boundary Bruce, yeah. Yes, he's now.
Played at Lucian's Pavilion there. But that was years ago. I was about 17 years old when I played.
Was that out over the water? What kind of a place was that?
It was out there on water, the lake. Right on the side of the lake, on the Asian lake.
Did they have regular dances there, just like a bar, or what was the place?
No, they had dances there. People would give picnics and then...
They had to pay to get the tickets to dance?
They had to have the pay to go in for the dance. They went to plays at the Pavilion.
Did you play just by yourself or with the band or what?
No, I played by myself.
You say you were about 17. How old are you now?
Six or five.
Sixty-five.
I'm six or five as old now.
That would be about 1912 again. He started playing when he was 10.
Yeah, that would be 19 and five about then. Do you remember any other piano players at that time that you heard? Any of their name or who they were?
Yeah, I know many piano players. There was George W. Thomas.
Oh, yeah, I've heard of him. He had some music in the company.
Yeah, he used to be a publisher, like reading and writing publishers.
New Orleans Hopscorp Blues. I know we... Houston Blues, a couple of others.
Clarence Williams. Frank Crump.
That's old man Frank Crump.
Yeah, old man Frank Crump. Johnny Charlie.
Saxe Paul and Planet Prayer would come up in my time. His daddy was talking about. Yeah.
Then...
Henry Julian's... Foreign-in-law. Then...
Johnny Charlie. Yeah.
Those fellas, what style did they play? Was it blues and ragtime both? Yes. Or just blues or how?
Played all... They all kind of played both. They played all kind of ragtime and everything else.
Popular tunes of the day.
Yeah, popular, yeah.
That includes such things as the Chalpiches and the Zerkers or anything like that?
Yeah, they played all that. Yeah, they played all that.
Yeah, they played all that.
And... Like myself, I used to play... I played blues at times. Another time I played all the songs. Jazz amount.
Yeah.
Played all the jazz. That's a shiny town. Down by the Old Mill Stream. Duh. Another song they used to play all the time. I used to like to play that. Span... In a little Spanish town.
Oh, yeah.
I remember that thing.
Did you have any numbers of your own that you used to play? Any blues of your own or anything like that?
No, I... I never did take that. I had another... Another blues my brother used to play. I used to play all the time. They called the Ham and Egg Blues.
Yeah, who used to play that?
My brother, Juby, used to play that. Called Ham and Egg Blues. He used to play that. I played that one night. But... And that at the Miles' place there. I was playing with... With... Louis Kepin.
Oh, the guitar player?

Yeah. Yeah. I played with Louis Kepin one night at that... At Head of the Miles' place. That was... Sanan in... In Decayla. They had a cabaret there. And I was playing there. And we played that Spanish town... About... Or recall man. About ten times we played that. I played that on piano.
Is that the place down by the French market? Yeah.
By the French market. Right by that's... Jackson Square. Right by that's Jackson Square.
Yeah. It's where Fernandez Wine Cellar is now. Is that the... A store that sells liquor?
I don't know what they got. I don't know what's there now. It'll be right at that corner. Right on the corner.
They got a liquor store right now.
What is that now? Yeah. They call that the Pond Alba building now.
Is that the...
No way. It wasn't saying to St. Peland. Yeah. St. Peland Decayla.
Yeah.
That's over on the other side. On the other side. St. Peland Decayla. There was... It was Eddie DeMauze there.
What is that name again?
Eddie DeMauze.
Eddie DeMauze.
Yeah.
Is that a French name or something?
That was an Italian fellow. Italian? Yeah. Italian fellow had a place. I played there a lot for him.
About when was that? Was that pretty early? Or was that the time of the Depression? Or after the First World War?
Or when would that be? That was after the First World War, yeah. After the First World War I played there.
By yourself or any band?

You said Louis Keppert. I played with Louis Keppert's band there. The whole band there? Yeah. We had Willis Addergo. Oh, yeah. Oh, I forget the other fellas was in the band. But I know them two. It was Willis Addergo and then Freddie Keppert. I was playing that one.
Freddie?
Yeah.
Is it Freddie or Louis?
Louis Keppert.
Louis.
That was Freddie Keppert's brother. Yeah. Freddie Keppert used to play the cornet. Freddie Keppert used to play the cornet at that time.
Did you ever hear Freddie play?
Oh, yeah.
You did hear him play?
Yeah, I heard Freddie play. Many times. Can you remember the very...
Oh, excuse me. For interrupting.

Freddie Keppert used to go riding on the trucks. They'd have a truck. They'd go riding on the band. They'd play on different corners. Freddie Keppert. And Louis Keppert. This... Joe Oliver. Oh, yeah. Kid Rene. And Buddy P.T.
Orange.

And Punch. Yeah, Punch. Chris Keppert. Yeah, Chris Kelly. You know, and I... That's that fella there. That's why I'd come to do Sharky Banana. That's why I'd come to do Sharky Banana, because I'd see Sharky... They used to go riding on the trucks with these fellas on Sunday. Sharky Banana to get on the truck with these fellas and go along, ride around in the truck and take his horn and go play.
He played with them on the truck.

Oh, yeah. He used to go around and Sharky was good. And one day we were sitting down. I was playing at Sharky's house on Miro Street. And Miro, between St. Peter and... and Cronelette walk there. I'd play him with him. And he used to play... sit down and play the card. Many times I played at Sharky's house. Yeah, he'd be sitting down there learning how to play the card.

Can you remember the very first band you ever heard? Any dance band? When you were a kid, say, five or ten years old, even before you started on Miro? What kind of bands, what kind of music did they have in the city then?
Oh, man. They had so many bands. The last kid they had, they had a bunch of bands. First round they were playing. It's like all the fellas called, the... the...
Keppert and Oliver.
Yeah, Keppert and Oliver. Emmanuel Perez.
Yeah.
Emmanuel Perez and... I don't remember the... They had Dave Dupes. They had the Dupes Band.
You remember...
They had the Rick Band. They had the Tuxedos. And, uh... And, uh...
What? You remember any of the parade bands? The Tuxedo, I guess, was on the street, too. Were they... Oh, yeah.

It was... Well, all of them... They'd be playing... different places. All around those parades and different things. But that was about, uh... the leading bands. I'm telling you, what I told you, that was about the leading bands they had at that time. that I remember.
Did you play with bands very much, Bill? Or did you play... No.

No, no. I played more by my... I played more by myself. I don't play... Most of the time I played by myself for all house parties. Yeah, house parties. I played for... All kinds of house parties. For white and colored.
Do you think...
Weddings and all things like that I played.
You played for the... for them dancing.
Oh, yeah. Dancing. Like, things like that I played.
Do you think if you... if you had a piano you could remember that ham and egg?
Oh, no. I don't believe I could play no more. I'm playing years. No. In years I played. I could... I don't believe I could play nothing no more.
When did you stop playing, Bill?
I stopped playing... about... oh, about... four years ago.
Oh, that's long, then.
Yeah. About four years ago, I quit.
Oh, that's a long time.
Yeah, I haven't played... I've played since then.

I don't... I don't think it's that long, but if you think... Yeah, it's that long. Because I played... I played with Frank... with Frank and Bill already. And I mean... Yeah, but... I mean, I was a young kid, around 12, 13 years old. I know that. But, uh... I don't know... 40 years old. I might be. But 40 years would be about 1920.

Frank... Frank was... Frank was playing, but I had quit. Yeah. Frank had quit, like Bruce, he said. You heard Bruce, but Bruce had... Bruce was... was... was playing... just about getting good, then, when I... Yeah. When I done quit, yeah.
It'll be by 1920, would you say? 1920 or the early 1920s?
No. Did you play as late as the Depression, when they had the WPA or anything that late?
No, I didn't play that, no. I wasn't playing on any of that Depression. I was working on the riverfront at that time. My hands at that time got stiff, I couldn't play no more.
Oh, is that where you stopped playing?

I stopped playing. There wasn't nothing in it. You go play all night for four or five hours, man. That was no money then. Oh, that didn't quit people getting all them jukeboxes and things around that time. They'd sooner dance by them jukeboxes. They didn't want to be bothered too much with the band.
Yeah.

And then when the, I believe that's when it's about the time they started forming them union. It was just about around that time, they started forming unions, and they said, you know, about the time I quit playing, about 45 years ago. That's when I quit playing.
Well, you were still a young man then when you quit playing.
Oh, yeah. Yeah, I quit. I couldn't play then, but I just stopped.
You'd be still in your twenties, do you think, when you stopped?
Oh, yeah.
You'd still be in your twenties.
Yeah, I'd say.
Do you remember one of the voice pieces that you learned on the piano?

The voice piece I learned on the piano all around. Oh, I don't know what the voice piece I was playing on the piano. But I played so many pieces. I could play anything, anything that was wrote. All I'd do is get the piece and whistle it, and I'd play it.
Did you ever learn to read music, or just always by air?
Always by air. No, never did read music. I just went on by air.
Do you remember any of the ragtime pieces, any of the rags that you played?
Under rags? Oh, I played most everything. I played most everything. Most every song that I believe was ever wrote. I played most every song that was wrote.
And those dances and those house parties you used to do, Did you have to play all the time, or did you play a certain number of pieces and then play?
Oh, you play a piece and stop giving people a chance to go around and walk around and buy a drink and something. Then wait a while, about 20, 30 minutes and play another piece like that, you know?
How long did you play when you did play? I mean, how long would the number last? How long did you play? Oh, you didn't.

You didn't play the more than about one voice, about two chords, sometimes three chords. Then stop. Give them a chance to take them and spend a little money, you know? Buy something to drink. A sandwich or something around there like that. Yeah. Then, uh...
Can you tell us any more about those house parties? Did they have them to make money or was it to pay, get money for their rent maybe or something? Or why did they...

No, I don't believe it was for the rent. I believe the people would do it more for the fun of us. Yeah. Give them the part of that. Get the children to pay to put the nickel up to come in. There would be a hoobah nickel to go in. Yeah. You know? Them chicks would come in and sell pop and, uh, lemonade and things like that for the church cake. Something like that. They'd all be in the nickels and pennies or drinks. They'd got no... I don't do it for some rent, no. At that time rent was too cheap. Rent was... Rent was from $3 a month. Really? From $3 a month to $6 a month. Yeah.
For the whole house?

Yeah, for the whole house. You could, uh... I remember the time when I was covered up there, about 25, 30 years old, and you could get a big, a great big two-story house with about 10 rooms for about $6 a month. But now you had to make that $6 a month. You had to work and hustle doggone good to get to make that $6 a month.
Yeah, the money was hard to get to do.

The house was there but there wasn't no way to make that. What's it what? Make 15 cents an hour. Yeah. Big man making 15 cents an hour, you know? Yeah, I think. That's, uh... You gotta figure on all that. No, I don't believe playing the piano like I used to do. And, uh... You know, the beginning of the party that I did, oh, it was not for the rest. It was more for the fun of it. Cause I played more... I played more for nothing than I played for money.
Yeah, that's true.

Cause I'd go around different places. I'd get around different ballrooms and... I'd, uh... See a fellow be playing. They had a job there. I'd... They just pitch in and say, well... They say, somebody say, here's Bill. Here come Bill. I'd walk on in there and say, well... Alright, Bill say, well, play a couple of pieces for me. And I'd just jump in and go and play a couple of pieces. And go and walk on out. Go somewhere else. I would never sit there all night unless I'd be playing myself.
Did they ever... Did you get many tips when you played those parties? Or just the play that they gave you?

No, not at them parties. You know, tips. You play some... You know, if you play in some ballroom or something, you get tips. That you play... Play in a ballroom or something like that for the people at night to draw the crowd, you know. That would, uh... That you'd get tips, I hear.
Did they ever advertise these parties or sell tickets in advance or anything?
No. They'd tell the people.
How did they know they were going to have those?
They'd just tell the children around. I'm going to give them a party Sunday. Yeah. They'd be telling the other ones when they'd come around. Sometime they'd have some big people.
I believe somebody told me once when they'd have a fish fry, didn't they hang a red lantern out or something? Yeah, red.

Yeah, you'd put a red light on the front. Yeah. You'd put a red light in front of the gate well in the evening, and the people pass there and see the lamp hanging there. Well, they'd know there was a fish fry there at night.
About the same as those parties or it's different when they have the fish fry?

Oh, well, you didn't have to put no light out for the party, no. Yeah. You'd just tell people, they'd come, most of the people just be coming along and they're playing. Yeah. You had to just see the butts in there dancing and they'd just give a nickel and come on in and dance. Yeah. Give a nickel and come on in there and dance. That's all I used to see about it. Yeah.
Did you ever get in any competition with other piano players?

Oh, yeah, that's all time to meet that. Oh, yeah? Oh, yeah, you know all the time. How did that work? You'd meet Lil Willa and you'd get in a place and what fella would be playing and then two, three might be there to play and everybody go to bucking one another. Did you take turns on the piano? Yeah, everybody take a turn, want to see who could play the best. Like I remember they had this Red Caillou, they had Lil Willa, they had Lil Kato and Big Kato, they had One Leg Alex Seed, and they had the old Blind Frank uptown. And myself, sometime we'd run across them uptown up there around the Garden District and we'd go on to bucking. Oh, and that fella too I'll forget to tell you about, Udell.
Oh, yeah, I'm afraid of him. What's his last name?
Oh, I done forgot, I'd forgotten either. I know Udell used to live up in Colton there. I'd run across him a couple of times and I'd play against him.
Well, did you have to play the same numbers or you could play your own numbers?
Just play with this play, and I'm going to play what you want. Just play what you want, and then the people that like it, they'd be classy about who's the best and who ain't the best.
How'd they decide? Did they clap real hard or judge or something?
Well, they'd be happy with Hollywood's the best and who ain't. Everybody, let me tell you we play the best, alright.
And Big Kato or Middle Kato, were they brothers or something?

Well, I'll tell you, I'll tell you, I had the biggest surprise of my time playing, the big surprise I had was one day I was, I passed one day up on Orleans Street. And at that time, I'd see the fellow because he was called Walter. And Walter used to be playing on the piano all the time. And I said, I got there and I said, well, he saw me, he said, Mr. Bill, he said, stop, he said, stop a minute, he said, yeah, I'm playing. He said, listen, let me play. He said, I'll play. And when I went inside, I fought with Walter Pichon. Oh, that's it. Oh, fat. And I sat down there and I listened to that boy playing. I told him, I said, boy, I said, you keep that up. I said, you'll be great someday. I said, you'll be one of the best they got you. I said, you put it good. I said, right now, there's very few in town can beat you. I said, Walt was just about, Walt was just about 12 years old then. And I told him that. He was living up here on Miro and Orleans at that time. I told him that.
He was hard to have. He played way different from what he's playing now. See, in that case, he played like baby Bruce and Boyle and different.

I told Walter, I said, he'd be great. But he did grow up to be good too. He said, I hear him 9, 11, 9, and I hear him over the television, on the radio, I hear him playing. He said, yeah, he's good. Walter's wonderful.
His brother often played very good too. Eddie Loomis. Remember Eddie Loomis?
No, I don't remember him good.
He could play pretty good. I don't remember him. Now, you were speaking about Big Kato and Little Kato.
Yeah.
Were they brothers or related?
It was the father and the son.
Oh, the royal son.
Oh, yeah, father and son. Oh.
They both played piano?
Yeah, both played the piano. That was good. Oh, man.
We always thought they were brothers.

Yeah, there was thousands of them. They had Eugene. They had Ornest Caress. White Newman. White Newman was about the best he had in the city at that time, him and Ornest Caress. Yes. At the time I tell you about when I was playing, White Newman would play anything. He'd play by note. White Newman, he'd play anything. I don't know if he's living yet or not. Or not. But Ornest Caress, I know he's dead.
Would they be about the same age as you?
Ornest would be a little older than me. But White Newman would be younger than me.
Oh, yeah.
Yeah. If he's living, he's younger than me.
If you see a con-patient band when they come on the television, that's your son playing trumpet.
Who?
White son.
White Newman.
No, no, no. No, no. No, no. No, no. No, no. No, no.

No. No. No. No. No. No. No. He was waking up on St. Charles Street there. I forget what number of the place now. He was waking up there on St. Charles Street up there at that time. Oh, I know thousands of piano players, but I couldn't call all their names. Yeah. But then they had, like, a long time. Before I started playing, there was hundreds of piano players around there and hundreds of musicians. And, like that old man, Pico that died there. Yeah. Old Alphonse Pico there. I remember him playing. But I was small when I heard him playing, you know, like Tiger Reg and High Society and all that. And I heard him, a fella taking it and playing that when I was little. And I played it myself after.
Do you remember who was the first one you ever heard play High Society, that clarinet part? Was it Pico or somebody else?
I heard Dave Dupass play on the clarinet. I heard Pico play that after, yeah. But the first one I ever heard played was Dave Dupass.
Do you remember George Bocquet clarinet player?
Oh, yeah, I remember Bocquet, yeah. I remember him. Yeah, I remember George Good. I remember George Bocquet, yeah.
And Sid DeVean.

Well, I know him too. I know Sid DeVean. I know Johnny Babe. I know Johnny Babe who could play cornet. Sid DeVean could play clarinet and cornet. I know. That's what I tell you. It would be hard now for me to tell you.
Do you remember one band from uptown that's supposed to be real early? Buddy Bolden. Do you remember Buddy Bolden?

Yeah, I remember Buddy Bolden's band. Yeah. I remember Buddy Bolden's band all around from about seven years old. I remember Buddy Bolden's band, yeah. Man, you bring it up so damn. Yeah. Remember where you heard them?
Where did they play? Or where did you hear them?
Oh, he had a piece there. He used to play about Buddy Bolden all the time. Oh, yeah. Yeah, he had a piece there. Take it away, huh?
Funky Button. Yeah, he used to play all.
I thought I was Buddy Bolden's band. He thought I was Buddy Bolden's band.
I thought I was Buddy Bolden's band.
I thought I was going to take it away. He used to play all of the things like that.
Do you remember where you heard him? Was he on the street or a wagon or a parade or something?
I was Buddy Bolden playing at the West End. At West End?
Yeah.
That's where I heard him play. I heard Charlie Charlie. Charlie Charlie used to play at the West End Tavis. He was in.
He was a piano player.

Piano player, yeah. I heard him, the first place I ever heard him playing outside of a house was out there at the West End Tavis. Out there on the Pulse Train Boulevard back then. That was years ago, though. Not right, not lately. An old man out there.
Do you remember Lincoln Park or Johnson Park when you were a kid? Yeah. Did you ever go out there? What was it like? Do you remember anything?
Big picnic ground out there.
It's not there now.
No, no.
I never did see them, either one.
Well, they had the Dixit Park, the Lincoln Park. They had the Commercial Park there. On the bayou, they had the Crosswood from there, they had the Southern Park.
What was the other one on the bayou?
The Commercial Park. Commercial. Commercial Lee Park. Right down the domain there in the bayou. Right across the street from there.
Out near City Park now, or is it this way from it?
That's right there. Right across the domain where the Bison joined it.
Yeah.
Right across there. Take up all that green there where you saw them houses there, Tallene Street.
Over in there?
All right, yeah. The Great Side of the City.
Yeah.
Just this way. It's a great big, all that where you saw them houses in there right now. That was the Commercial Park there.
Yeah.
And on that side, right on that side of it this way, was the Southern Park. It would be open from, it would be open from Domain Street, clear to the bayou.
For those for color, for whites, could everybody go?

Everybody go, for color, then white. No, there was no segregation in there, anything like that. Color, everything white used to go. And, uh, at the same way at the lake, you'd go out to the lake, and everybody would go. White and color used to be out there.
At West End, too?
West End, too. West End, you know. About that Spanish food and Millenburg.
What about Millenburg, like this place, Lucian's, that you told about, is that for white or color?
That was a colored place. It was a colored place. Yeah, colored man only.
Yeah.
Lucian had flying horses and everything out there. Mm-hmm. Little people arrived. Yeah.

I was going to ask them more about the parks. Did they have dance bands and dancing at those parks? Yeah. Like the park and commercial park? Yeah, they had different bands, plays. Did you ever play at any of those parks?
Oh, no, no, I haven't played in them parks, no. Never played in them parks.
Somebody told us...
I played at the lake.
Yeah, out at the lake.
Yeah, out at the lake.
Somebody told us they used to have balloons to go up. What do you have? I think it's part. Do you remember any of those?

Yeah, I remember the... We used to go out there and look at a fellow called... Billy Caillou, I believe it was. He used to go up in that balloon. Jump out that balloon. He had to go up there and then jump out that thing.
Jump out in a parachute.
Yeah, jump out. Oh, but they ain't had no parachute like they got today. A man's most safe than he said they got today than what he had.
What did he have, bro?

Huh? That great big old thing looked more like a sheet than anything else what he had there coming down with. It looked like no parachute. Yeah. That's right, man. Oh, man, look at that fellow. It looked like he'd go about a thousand feet, about a thousand feet up there. I'd get over the park and then fall out that thing. And that man would come down. You know, after he'd fall out sometime, he'd fall in a tree or anything around there. The other days, I'd see them hug the tree and the balloon traveling. Come way up here in town, they'll blow from way back there. Fall on top of a house or something. People get up there and catch a balloon to get a dollar.
Yeah.
Fall, you catch a balloon, you get a dollar.
Something like you catch a ball at the ball, fall, you go in free.
You go in for nothing when you get the ball out to be outside. I remember that good. You see that train? They had a train used to run out to the Spanish food. A bangle train.
Oh, which I knew about Smokey Mary. It went out on the Asian field. This is a different train.

No, I'm talking about the train used to run there on Bemmel Street. Yeah. It would run there. It would run from Rampart, from Basin and Canal. It would come on out through the track out there, the Sedlose Street. And it would go on out there behind the City Park and make that tour. They would go out on the street to the lake.
In fact, a steam engine, not a street car.
No steam engine.
Steam engine. Did they have a name for that? Like Smokey Mary for a little bit.
No, it was called out the Bemmel train.
Bemmel train.
Yeah, it was Spanish food. It was running Spanish food.
Yeah. Maybe I heard of it. I forgot about it.
Go to Spanish food. Go away or not on the Cave Charles wall. And switch and come on back in town.
Yeah.

Come on back in town. I forgot how much that was. I forgot how much that was to go out there. How long did it take? Nickel or die on the ride out there. Oh, man. It looked like you had an hour or two to get out there.
That's kind of slow. Did they make a lot of stops along the way?

Yeah, pick up people. Yeah, a lot of different stops. They pick up the people and bring them to the lake. Come back and say, well, it's time to put them off. Well, they had bands of music be playing out there on Sunday then. There was bands of music playing. And I was small. I remember that. I was about six, seven years old, I guess, when I was going out to the lake on the train.
Can you remember what the music was like? Was it ragtime or more classical music or marches? Or what was it like?
Oh, more ragtime music. It's like they jazzed them up today. They jazzed them up at that time. It wasn't much different, isn't it?
Not the same, yeah.
Yeah. Boys, this now, look like more than other people, everything they get, they go on the jazz.
Yeah.

See, they just jazzed most everything. Like them old-time charlots. I used to play a whole lot in charlots. There was a piece there they called Membrance. They called it Membrance. I remember they played that in the charlots. You could play in charlots, you could play in waltz. You mean they made a popular tune out of it? You mean they made a popular tune out of it? Yeah, but for waltzing, you know. Yeah, made popular tune out of it. For waltzing.
But you remember it way back as a shottee?
Oh, yeah. I remember way back that piece.
You remember any of the quadrilles? Did you ever play quadrille dancing?

No. No, I never played quadrille. I seen it done. Seen them dance the quadrille. But no, I never did play that. Never did play that. I remember there was a woman from... There was two women come from up around... Somewhere up in Illinois. There was two men. They were very tall. They used to dance at the quadrille line. They used to dance at them theaters down there.
What is it?
Yeah, quadrille. Just regular... Dancing for them, you know. Like a stage production. Yeah, for stages. That's where you go there and then. Like all that Black Paddy show and all that.
Oh, yeah. I've heard about that.
All that. They used to come to them big theaters. They'd come down there.
I was going to ask some more about the blues. When is the first time you ever heard the blues? Before you played or after you learned to play? When did you first hear blues?
Man, I heard them blues from a baby. I wasn't playing blues.
You were a baby.
Yeah. Blues. I believe the blues was up to whoever comes here. I believe they found the blues. Yeah, when they come here. I believe they found the blues in the car.
What kind of blues is it? Did people sing them or play them on guitar?

Oh, they'd sing them, play them with a band. Play them piano everywhere. You know, when you go, you could hear the blues. Different instruments. People would play them. Yeah, there were people that played that. Play them blues. I don't remember that show, man. Blues was out before I was born. Yeah.
I just wondered if maybe you heard it very early.

Played and singing the blues and dancing the blues and things like that. People just got on out there and just made their own words and just put them up there and go to sing it. That's all I was. That's how far I can remember the blues. So everybody come here, everybody come here about 65 years. I knew they was here because I was born 65 years ago and I come here, I found the blues here.
Is blues supposed to be happy music or sad music or what kind of music is it?

Well, I believe it's happy for them that like them. I believe most of the people will go for that blues, yeah. Right now, you take the day. I never heard as many blues. When I was coming up, it's what they got today.
Yeah, the rock and roll is really all blues.
Everybody turn around and have somebody got a blues or somebody making a new one.
Everybody turn around. When people were dancing the blues, were they having a good time? They were enjoying themselves?

Oh, yeah. You could dance that in one step or two step. Other than people, that's how they danced that, one or two step. They're playing them sometimes. And they had another dance they called a slow drag.
Yeah, I've heard of that. Is that slower than the blues?
Yeah, but that was slow. You'd be dancing blues like that, but you was dancing slow. Yeah, real slow. They call it slow drag. That's that.
You always played the blues slowly?

Well, sometimes. Sometimes you play them slow. Sometimes you didn't. I like that Chinatown up here. People used to be playing around in China. They could play that two, three different ways. They could play that in Chinatown. I like, when I used to play Chinatown, I could take them and play it in the waltz town. And as I played in the waltz town, then turn right around and jazz and all that. People think I'd be playing two different pieces. That'd be the same song. They'd be playing in the waltz town. None of them be jamming. I'd do that with most of them, pieces I used to play.
Could you do that with blues too, Bill?

Oh, yeah. You could play the blues fast if you wanted. Yeah, there's fast blues. You could play them. It'll learn to play them fast and slow. Get your time in the waltz. The best I've seen about it, the best I know about it. I know everybody had a good time. Everywhere the blues was played, everybody seemed to have a good time.
You couldn't play the blues. There was no use of playing, no.
Oh, no.
In other words, it's not really necessarily always sad music.
No. No, no. The blues, I don't sing about no blues that's sad. No.

No. You know how blues get sad? Like if somebody maybe broke up with their sweetheart or something like that, and somebody sing the blues or something like that, that's where it gets sad. Other than that, it's different.

You know what I think the blues is sad? It's after somebody that got broke and drunk and lost all that money. That got broke and drunk and lost all that money. Then he'd get the blues. Everything was sad from then. Yeah.
Yeah.
Yeah, yeah.
Do you remember any blues singers, especially singers when you were a kid, or even a little later when you were growing up? Oh, no. Did it real good from here?
Man, they had both people who sing the blues out of them. I couldn't remember. Oh, I don't know.

Did you ever hear any of the singers from away from here that came in the theaters like Ma Rainey, or say Mamie Smith, or different ones that might have come through here singing at a theater, or on a show, or anything?
I don't remember them people. I heard of them, yeah. As many I went and seen, I couldn't call a name. I wasn't seen at different theaters.
By the way, did you ever travel around in any kind of a show, or carnival, or go away from here to play at all in music?

No, I never did leave yet. Never did leave? No, I never did leave yet, especially to go play nowhere, no. But I was in Chicago one time, man, and I played my way out of there. I played my way out of the White Castle Cabaret one night there. I was broke, and then I said this and I went on playing the Yala Dog Blues, the Southern Cross of the Yala Dog Blues. I started playing them, and I'd pick up about five or six dollars around that collection.
About how old were you when you were in Chicago?
Oh, I was about...
Is that before the war, or after the war?
Oh, that was before the war. I was about 19 years old then. I was between 19 and 20 years old then.
Did you hear any other music, Chicago bands? Were they any...
Oh, there was plenty of them up there.
Were they any different than the New Orleans bands, much difference in the music?

Yeah, plenty different. Yeah, they did. Up there at that time, they just didn't have the jazz that was down there. They just didn't have it. They didn't have it. No, they didn't have the jazz that was down there. They didn't have it at that time. I'd been since... Lately since, uh... Louis Armstrong and them fellas been going up that way, but they've been getting all that different jazz. Yeah. But up that time when I was around in there, they didn't have it then.
Did you ever meet any other New Orleans musicians that you knew? In Chicago?
Oh, well, plenty of them.
Oh, yeah.
But they was all out for themselves. They couldn't do nothing for me. Yeah, they couldn't do nothing for me. Were they playing?
Were they working?

When I was over there, Louis Armstrong hadn't come there then. No. No, Louis Armstrong hadn't been there. If they tell you that night, I got around that cabaret and I wanted to leave. I wanted to leave Chicago. I wanted to come home. I didn't have no money. And I got around there and I started playing the Meala Dog Blues in that white cabaret. And I... stuff

picked up about five or six dollars around there and I got that little change and I hoboed my way had enough to buy enough food to come on down and I hoboed my way all the way from Chicago back here took me about six days to do it but I done it, I come on back I was in St. Louis I played I was playing the Beale Street Blues then when I was in I played the Beale Street Blues, I played the Yardin' Down Blues in St. Louis it was in old man's place that old gray man up there, they called Bailey, I played in his place about four or five nights in St. Louis and I left there I left St. Louis there was nothing more than that, it looked like I couldn't make nothing there and I come on back tips wasn't so good then I didn't left there and come on back see the boats of the places that you'd be playing they wouldn't hire so they wasn't getting no siren so you just had to figure out what you'd pick up around
did you hear any good ragtime players in St. Louis?

oh yeah they had plenty of good musicians there and so the fact they had better musicians in St. Louis at that time than they had in Chicago it was jazz music yeah they had better ones in St. Louis than they had in Chicago stuff stuff stuff
stuff stuff stuff !

around Mark Street, there was a, I remember there was being some kind of a ballroom or cabaret there. The man had piano players around about a thousand. Yeah, there had piano players around about a thousand. They say it in your head. They say piano players. They say piano in your head was there. That was no trouble about a piano player. They say, well, I can't do it. You didn't have to, you didn't have to do a trumpet if I had to play. You could, this go up most of any corner and you could find somebody who could play. That's how I tell you, when the jukebox started coming in, they started putting the jukebox on the corner playing for nickel. It's the same way as when organ grinding was coming around. The big house party would be going on. And organ grinding would get on the corner and grind that organ and play it. Everybody run out the party and organ playing. Yeah, I played organ. On the corner. That's how that goes. It wasn't that.
I was going to ask about some of the contests again. Do you remember any of the pieces you would use when you'd win a contest? What were your best numbers that you'd play?

Oh, the High Society. The High Society, I could take it, I could take it, and run, put the head on the bottom of that High Society. I could play that piece. Yeah, when I was playing, I could play the High Society good. It had all the pause there.
Any other special numbers that you had?
Oh, the High Society, I had the Chinatown, in a little Spanish town. Oh, put the head on, any song.
Yeah. So you didn't like any number of your own, any special number of your own?
Oh, I didn't have no special number for myself.
Yeah.
Just go on and play.

Oh, that reminds me, the other day, baby Bruce was saying that at the end, they put on a little stop, as he called it, a special little ending. Every player had their own ending. Did you have your own ending,
do you remember? Oh, yeah. You couldn't find five fellas that stopped the light. Everyone would put a little jazz on and then and stop.
Did you have your own...
Oh, yeah. Well, everybody had their own way, a way of winding up there. You had their own way of winding up.
Remember sort of how yours go, can you hum it out or anything?

Yeah, you say, go on there and put your fancy touch on the back of it and then stop. Everybody's quitting, go to clap. You go to clap, but they're clapping up there and when you know they like it, you play another chorus over. Go on and even get it, even take another little short dance out like that. Go on.
Who do you think was about the best piano player you ever heard or maybe the best two or three piano players you ever heard in your life?

Well, I'm going to tell you. The best I heard play piano was Frank Crump for number one. I take Clarence William. Take Clarence William. And well, George W. Thomas, he could play, but he couldn't play, he wouldn't play much. He'd go more publishing and writing and publishing. Then they had another one a good piano player there. I don't want to name my brother Juby because everybody in town thought he was the best.
He really is.
Oh yeah, everybody thought my brother Juby in town was the best. But I thought the bands without name there, I thought they could play better than my brother.
You mentioned Dwight Newman.
Dwight Newman was good. He was playing, he used to play about notes, but he wasn't playing with the time of these bands I'm talking about. Oh, I see. Dwight Newman come up here lately.
Later, yeah.
Yeah, lately. Him and Nguyenus Caress and all that.
Did you ever hear a piano player called Tony Jackson when you were a kid?
Yeah. Yeah, I remember Tony Jackson.
How was he?
Tony Jackson was a good piano player. Yeah, Tony Jackson was a good piano player. In fact, Tony Jackson was the only piano player I would sing. The first one I would sing when he played.
Some people tell me he used to work in the district too.
Yeah, he played all around the district and everywhere. Tony Jackson. Did you ever work
in the district in any of these playing piano in any of those houses?

No, I played around a whole lot of like Pete Lala's in different places around there. I played around in different places but I wasn't on no side of them. Just go around and different people playing. Now, around in all in that Vicarae up there I played many places I played in.

Is there anything you can tell us about John Lala's place, the Big 25? They just tore that down a few years ago. I remember it. I never heard any music or anything. Did they have music ever at the Big 25 much?
No.
On Franklin Street there?
No. There wasn't much music there. No. That was multiple gambling places and drinking places. Where Lala was on Arborville and Liberty.
That was the Pete Lala's place.
Yeah, Pete Lala. Pete Lala had that place. There were he had the cabaret. There were the dancers used to go in the cabaret there. Is that Liberty
or Marais you remember for sure? Some people told me Marais somebody.

No, he had a place on Vembley. He had a place lately there but it was just like a little bit of dance hall but there was no cabaret where he had it. The big cabaret was on Liberty in Arborville. Living in Arborville Pete Lala had that. There was Butterbean and Susie used to be there was Butterbean and Susie used to be in there. I used to go around there sometime and look at Butterbean and Susie be singing along there.
I remember them.
Yeah, well I used to go in there sometime and look at the show a while and then come on back from there. I'd sit down there and listen at them to play.
Did you ever know this cabaret called Whining Boy around town? Who? Whining Boy.
No.
Some people later called himself Jelly Roll Jelly Roll Martin. Do you remember?
No, I don't know him. No, I don't know him.
Did you ever know Professor Manero, Emmanuel Manero?
Yeah, I remember him.
You remember him?

Yeah, I remember him. I remember him good. In fact, I know a whole lot of musicians, but I know a whole lot of them when they started. They do a whole lot of them when they wind up. Like Tony Almanric, I remember Tony Almanric when he didn't know who the horn was. Tony Almanric, his dad had a big boat I tried to buy. Oh,
yeah?

Yeah, a big house boat I tried to buy one time. The old man would go out there and have his presence sit out there. See, he'd be sitting out there sometimes reading his paper for that boat. He'd be spent putting out the whole summer out there his dad. He was riding around in the skip, playing in the bay, riding at that island. That old number of island back there. He'd be around paddling in the skipper. I knew he wasn't set about playing no horn then at that time. I remember that.
He'd be just a little kid then.
Yeah, just about that high.
He'd be

about that high. I'm a rick. sharky, he was riding. Sharky, he wasn't set about playing no sharky a long time before he started playing on. But when he did get a start at it, he just went right on through with it. He'd play with Buddy P.T. and Baird Perez and Punch and Big Joe Oliver. He'd just play with any one of them trucks would come along. The first one would come, he'd just jump on and go on with them fellas and go on and play.
Did you ever play one of those advertising jobs? Did they ever have a piano on the truck?
Sometimes some of them some of them had piano on them. See, when they played the piano, the piano would lead.
Oh, yeah?
Yeah, the corner wouldn't lead. The piano would lead when they had a piano on the truck.
What would the corner do? Play harmony ?

He'd come there, he'd be blowing. He'd blow, but the piano was the leader. He'd go there and he'd play. I see now today, everything in the day is cornered leading. The most of the time they didn't have cornered, they had trumpets. They were blowing trumpets at that time. The short ones? Yeah, the short ones they were playing, they were called a trumpet. And cornered come out, I believe, C.G. Conn's is the first one started that Conn headband.

I was going to ask you more about the piano players. Did most of all these other piano players, you said there were a thousand around here, did they come from town or some of them come from out of town, the country or Florida or along the coast, Gulf, coast,
where they
come from?
Most of the piano players I know around here was right from here.
Born right here.

Yeah, born and raised right here. there was a fellow downtown, I was forgetting him, they called Sam Galata. Sam Galata, yeah. Sam Galata was a good piano player, he played by notes. But he used to play all that kind of fashion music, you know. Didn't believe in playing no blues and all that. He used to play all book music. Sam Galata, he used to hang around down there by the alley. He was a good piano player.
The alley, was that where Sam Bernard was?
Yeah, Sam Bernard in the Claymore. Yeah, right in behind there. There's a place called the alley there. Well, that's where he used to be playing around there.
Did most of these piano players, did any of them make their living from the piano or did have to have other day jobs, some other trade or something?

Most of them had jobs. Yeah, the most of them had a house of playing and they had jobs on the side. I always figured out. I never didn't know if none of them had no this maker of living out there. Lately, these fellas just started taking an out and playing since this union came up.
Yeah,

they fella could make enough money to take care of himself. But all before that know a man had to have a job. Yeah, a man had to have a job. He played piano, he never make it. Not survive long as I did. That long there. Take a long and just play piano, play piano. If I figured I would be here a long time ago.
I
quit in time. I see the place where I was going to start to that. We know the piano said. Oh, did. did. He played a piano.
When
you
started out playing, did you have to practice much? Did you have to work hard at it?

I didn't come in like that and sit down and fool around and play a little bit, go along in the street and play, run on to school, come on back, I'd sit down a little bit, about hours like that and throw the piano and get up and go on about a bit. I found out I was a good piano player and I didn't know it myself. I didn't know I could play that good myself. Plenty of people tell me I could play. I just play move for kicks out of the

Every time I played Set and Set a Piece, I'd just jump up there and go on and play it. I'd get up there and go to play it. The very times I got in places there, a fellow would say, Do you know this piece? I'd say, Bill, you can play Set and Set a Piece. I'd say, Well, whistle it. I'd say, You whistle it. They'd whistle it, I'd go on and play it. That's all I'd done. They'd whistle a piece, I'd go on and play the piece.
It didn't take you long then to learn it or practice on it or anything?

No, I didn't have to practice. If you'd whistle it, I'd play it. I'd play it right off if you'd whistle it. That's how I used to play it. It didn't bother them. There's no worries all about me playing together.
When you played those house parties, did you usually take the front off the piano? I know that baby Bruce had the front and the top off his piano. Was that the usual thing?

No, no. That wasn't necessary. I'd say, Plenty of people, they'd do it to make the sound come out. I'll tell you another thing they used to do. To make the piano sound like a drum. You could hear the piano and the drum. They'd get a big piece of paper, and they'd put behind them the strings, behind the keys. They'd been hit on them. You had a tap on the paper from the keys, and you had the string playing the music. Plenty of people do that. A lot of them would open the front of the piano there, and they'd take that front off there and throw it back. But that was unnecessary. If you could play, you could play.
Yeah, sure.
Yeah, you'd always make the sound come out. The best thing about it is to get there and sit down and play. And know what you was doing. That's all I said about it.
Yeah, did you use the pedals much on the piano?
No.
Didn't bother with it.

No, I didn't have to bother with the pedal on the piano. I don't bother with that too much. You need to, uh, if you got on a good piano, if you got on a good piano, you had, you had all you wanted there. With all them keys they had in front of you. You had all you wanted with all them keys they had in front of you, you got on a good piano. That's all I said.
Did you use a lot of left hand, a lot of bass? Big Bruce said he was known for using his left hand quite a bit.

Oh, yeah, I could do it. Keep his left hand, his left hand. Yeah, well, you see, but you could take and, you could take and just sit there and play the blues and different things, short hand. Just play them right in the short. Then another time, you just take long, you lose long basses. Oh, yeah. And just use them swinging basses. Well, that's most of the time when you go into jazzing. When you're going to really jazz out of peace, you take and you use that long bass. And if you just could play it long, slow, and play the bottom of the play, well, you just go along and play. You didn't have to take and use some swinging basses in there. You didn't have to use a swing bass. Once you use a swing bass is when you would be jazzing a piece. You watch most of the piano players a day, how to do it. If they're not going to take and jazz a piece, you see how they play in short. And they take and, when they go to jazz and you see that hand, that hand will get a whip and whether they want it or not, that hand is going. Yeah, they know right where it's going. And after you play that piece, you can turn all around and be looking and talking to everybody. That hand is going to go in the right place. It ain't going to go in the wrong place. You don't have to see it. The eagle's apple is going to the right place where it belongs. And that's amazing.
Would you rather play by yourself or have a drummer, a guitar or something with you? How do you feel?

Well, it used to feel good sometimes when you get the guitar and drumming all that alongside your corner when you be playing. It feels good. The best thing for a fella who was out there playing, he'd go on by himself.
Yeah.

Yeah, he'd go on by himself. And his praise would be getting, he'd get it. There are people talking about you, about you playing four or five days or maybe five or six years. There are people talking about you and they'd be talking about you and they wouldn't know it was you. You'd be right there sitting down and listening down. And they wouldn't know it's you. They heard you playing. They wouldn't know it.
They wouldn't remember your name.
They wouldn't recognize you. They'd be talking about you and you'd be sitting down there listening to that.
That's about the end of this tape.

segments.title: Opening of the interview and Thompson's birth
segments.summary: Russell opens the tape with date and address at Thompson's home, naming those present. Thompson gives his birth in 1895 on Claiborne Street.

segments.title: Father the banjo player on the West End and lake boats
segments.summary: Thompson's father played banjo in bands at West End and later on pleasure boats at Milneburg, with Joe Murphy named as a bandleader.

segments.title: Learning piano from brother Juby, no lessons
segments.summary: He picked up piano around age ten from his older brother Juby, never took lessons, and played ragtime and blues, making each piece his own way.

segments.chapter: First jobs and the piano scene
segments.title: First jobs: Cronlite Walk and Lucian's Pavilion at the lake
segments.summary: His first jobs were house parties, a place on Cronlite Walk (Lafitte Street) and Lucian's Pavilion on the lake at about 17, always playing solo.

segments.chapter: First jobs and the piano scene
segments.title: Other piano players and the popular repertoire
segments.summary: Thompson names George W. Thomas, Clarence Williams, Frank Crump and others; they played ragtime, blues and popular tunes, and he lists tunes he liked.

segments.chapter: First jobs and the piano scene
segments.title: Ham and Egg Blues and playing with Louis Keppard at a cabaret
segments.summary: He recalls Juby's Ham and Egg Blues, and a night with Louis Keppard at a cabaret near the French Market, playing Spanish Town repeatedly.

segments.chapter: First jobs and the piano scene
segments.title: Playing for Eddie DeMauze with Louis Keppard's band
segments.summary: After the First World War he played often at an Italian man's place, in Louis Keppard's band with Willis Addergo; they clarify Louis versus Freddie Keppard.

segments.chapter: First jobs and the piano scene
segments.title: Freddie Keppard and the band trucks; Sharkey learning cornet
segments.summary: Thompson heard Freddie Keppard and others play from advertising trucks, and recalls Sharkey riding the trucks and practicing at his house on Miro Street.

segments.chapter: First jobs and the piano scene
segments.title: First bands he heard as a child
segments.summary: Asked about earliest bands, he lists Keppard, Oliver, Perez, Dupas, the Rick band and the Tuxedos as the leading bands.

segments.title: Playing solo for house parties and weddings
segments.summary: He mostly played alone at house parties for white and colored people, weddings and dances.

segments.title: When and why he stopped playing
segments.summary: He says he quit playing, tracing it to stiff hands, riverfront work, jukeboxes, low pay and the new union, while Dejan tries to date it.

segments.title: Playing by ear and the rhythm of a house party
segments.summary: He never read music, played any tune he could whistle, and describes playing a piece then pausing so people could buy drinks.

segments.title: Why house parties were held and how little they paid
segments.summary: House parties were for fun, with a nickel at the door; rent was a few dollars a month yet money was scarce, and he often played for nothing.

segments.title: Tips, spreading the word, and the red lantern fish fry
segments.summary: Tips came in ballrooms but not parties; parties were announced by word of mouth, and a red light marked a fish fry.

segments.title: Piano competitions and bucking contests
segments.summary: Pianists took turns to see who was best; he names Red Cayou, Little Willie, the Katos, One-Leg Alex and Blind Frank.

segments.title: Hearing young Walter Pichon
segments.summary: Thompson recalls hearing the twelve-year-old Walter Pichon on Orleans Street and predicting he would be great.

segments.title: Big and Little Kato, Ornest Caress and White Newman
segments.summary: The Katos were father and son; he rates White Newman and Ornest Caress among the best of the time, with an exchange about Newman's son.

segments.title: Alphonse Picou, Dave Dupas and High Society clarinet
segments.summary: He recalls Picou, says Dave Dupas was the first he heard play the High Society clarinet part, and acknowledges Bocquet and Sid DeVean.

segments.title: Hearing Buddy Bolden's band at West End
segments.summary: He remembers Bolden's band from about age seven, hearing it at West End, plus Charlie Charlie playing piano there.

segments.title: Lincoln, Johnson, Commercial and Southern parks
segments.summary: He describes the big picnic parks and where Commercial Park and Southern Park stood relative to the bayou.

segments.title: No segregation at the parks and lake; Lucian's a colored place
segments.summary: The parks and lake were open to all; Lucian's at Milneburg was for colored people only, and he played only at the lake.

segments.title: Balloon ascents and parachute jumps
segments.summary: He recalls watching a man go up in a balloon and jump with a crude parachute, and people catching balloons for a dollar.

segments.title: The Bemmel steam train to the lake
segments.summary: He describes the steam train that ran from Basin and Canal out to the lake, slow, with bands playing on Sundays, when he was six or seven.

segments.title: Ragtime, jazzing old tunes, waltzes and quadrilles
segments.summary: The early music was ragtime that people jazzed up; he played tunes as waltzes and charlotte pieces, never quadrilles, though he saw stage quadrille dancers.

segments.title: When he first heard the blues
segments.summary: He says he heard the blues from infancy, sung and played everywhere, made up by people with their own words.

segments.title: Dancing the blues, slow drag, and whether blues are sad
segments.summary: He explains one-step, two-step and slow drag, playing a tune several ways, why blues are not necessarily sad, and that he cannot name blues singers.

segments.title: Hoboing from Chicago after playing in a cabaret
segments.summary: Aged about 19 he was broke in Chicago, played blues in a white cabaret for fare money, and found Chicago lacked New Orleans jazz.

segments.title: St. Louis on the way home and its piano players
segments.summary: On the trip back he played in Bailey's place in St. Louis for several nights, found better musicians there than in Chicago, and compares pianists everywhere to jukeboxes.

segments.title: His best numbers and everyone's own ending
segments.summary: His contest pieces were High Society, Chinatown and Spanish Town, and each player had his own fancy ending.

segments.title: The best piano players he heard
segments.summary: He ranks Frank Crump and Clarence Williams first, mentions George W. Thomas and his brother Juby, and Dwight Newman as later.

segments.title: Tony Jackson and the district
segments.summary: He remembers Tony Jackson as a fine pianist who played in the district; he himself never worked a district house regularly.

segments.title: Pete Lala's cabaret and the Big 25
segments.summary: Little music at the Big 25, but Pete Lala's cabaret on Liberty and Arbor had a show with Butterbeans and Susie.

segments.title: Professor Manetta, Tony Almerico and Sharkey as a child
segments.summary: He knew Manetta, remembers Tony Almerico as a child, and recalls Sharkey going on trucks with various players.

segments.title: Piano on the advertising trucks
segments.summary: When a truck had a piano, the piano led rather than the cornet; he adds a remark about trumpets and cornets.

segments.title: Where the piano players came from; Sam Galata
segments.summary: Most pianists were born locally; he describes Sam Galata, who played only written music, near the alley.

segments.title: Making a living at piano
segments.summary: Most pianists held day jobs; only after the union could one live from playing.

segments.title: Never practiced: playing anything he heard whistled
segments.summary: He did not practice, found he played well by accident, and could play any piece someone whistled.

segments.title: Piano technique: front off, pedals and left hand
segments.summary: He says taking the piano front off was unnecessary, describes paper behind strings for a drum sound, no pedals, and short versus swinging bass.

segments.title: Preferring to play alone; end of tape
segments.summary: He prefers to play alone, noting people praise you without knowing it is you; Russell ends the tape.
